items.title: Before Jules Verne, Edgar Allan Poe imagined the Space Age
items.summary: It may be tempting to dismiss out of hand the notion that Edgar Allan Poe — popularly conceived of today as an almost mythic figure cloaked in ravens and tell-tale hearts — was the “grandfather of realistic spaceflight fiction” and had a significant effect on the conceptual development of the spacecraft. But it is no tall tale. The young orphan who walked the night-lit streets of Baltimore, the first American city with gas streetlamps, had a mind that strove to encompass not only the macabre but the entirety of the cosmos. His greatest work, in his own opinion, was not one of his popular mysteries or phantasmagorias but his prose poem Eureka , which originated as his 1848 lecture titled “The Cosmography of the Universe.” His tale of a voyage to the Moon, “The Unparalleled Adventure of One Hans Pfaall,” first published in 1835, was almost as dear to his heart, claiming that it was the first plausible application of scientific principles to the problem of travel between worlds. Although the boastful Poe oversold his claim, his was indeed the first to remove the veil of satire and focus on the details of the voyage itself. His was also the first, perhaps unsurprisingly, to explore some of the darker aspects of the psychological motivations for spaceflight, and he was the first to situate his spacecraft firmly within the context of mundane economics and engineering. The result was that “Hans Pfaall” became an animating spirit of interplanetary adventure to others — most notably Jules Verne, who, 30 years later, inspired by its visitation upon him, would follow in Poe’s gothic wake to the Moon. As a famed American original, the study of Poe has engendered a voluminous literature, as has “Hans Pfaall.” From the perspective of spaceflight history, however, several of its important contributions remain underappreciated. [For instance], Poe’s descriptions of the preparations, as well as of the voyage itself, take up the majority of the 46-page story, with Pfaall arriving at the Moon only on page 43. He also took pains to situate his work within the context of the spaceflight concepts that had come before. In his own “Note on Hans Pfaall,” a document as significant as the story itself — as it is the first American essay on the conceptual development of spaceflight — Poe references and reviews his predecessors, from Lucian [of Samosata] to [George] Tucker. The rather arrogant Poe was decidedly dismissive of almost everyone — calling Tucker’s [story of a voyage to the Moon] “deplorably ill conceived” and Cyrano de Bergerac’s tales “utterly meaningless” — with the exception of [Francis] Godwin, whose work he felt was “somewhat ingenious.” Poe’s opinions and proclamations here are less interesting than the fact that there is already a recognition, even in the Baltimore of 1839, of a community of ideas related to the problem of spaceflight that had been developing for generations. Although he considered himself in conversation with these other spaceflight authors, albeit somewhat belligerently, the principal influences for “Hans Pfaall” were scientific ones. It was Poe’s enthusiasm for contemporary astronomy that motivated his interest in the concept of spaceflight, and this had similarly inspired Richard Adam Locke’s famous Great Moon Hoax in the same year. Indeed, Poe treated John Herschel’s popular A Treatise on Astronomy , published in America in 1834, as his textbook, relying on it as his primary source of information about the distance, angles, and orbits required for a voyage to the Moon. Although a small step, he was the first to take a specific astronomy text and use it to provide a rough technical description of a lunar mission architecture — one that was sufficiently detailed that it could later be diagrammed by Nikolai Rynin in his pioneering 1928 spaceflight encyclopedia. Poe would claim that the design in “Hans Pfaall” was “original, inasmuch as regards an attempt at verisimilitude, in the application of scientific principles (so far as the whimsical nature of the subject would permit), to the actual passage between the earth and the moon.” To the extent that this was the case, it was due significantly to his application of contemporary astronomical knowledge. Although the engineering approach presented in “Hans Pfaall” for getting to the Moon — an enclosed balloon-borne carriage with a pneumatic air condenser — has often been dismissed as technically naive, it was actually grounded in Poe’s reading of contemporary astronomy. For example, the pneumatic air condenser — which is the core innovation of Poe’s spacecraft, and which flows from Hans Pfaall’s profession as a bellows maker — is able to function because, as Poe points out, recent astronomical observations had suggested that interplanetary space might have a very thin atmosphere that could potentially be condensed into breathable air with the right technology. For this, Poe points to the zodiacal light and to Benjamin Valz’s observation of the decreasing period and diminished coma of Encke’s comet when it was near the Sun. Valz proposed that this was the result of a resisting medium, an atmosphere that surrounded the Sun, and Poe’s Pfaall simply extended this notion, positing that the zodiacal light was this atmosphere: “It appeared to me evidently in the nature of a rare atmosphere extending from the sun outwards, beyond the orbit of Venus at least, and I believed indefinitely farther. Indeed, this medium I could not suppose confined to the path of the comet’s ellipse, or to the immediate neighborhood of the sun. It was easy, on the contrary, to imagine it pervading the entire regions of our planetary system, condensed into what we call atmosphere at the planets themselves.” Other references to the theories and observations of contemporary astronomy abound. When, during his 19-day journey to the Moon, Pfaall encounters explosive debris, he presumes it to have come from one of the many volcanoes on the lunar surface, in accord with the volcanic explanation for the moon’s pockmarked appearance that was the dominant theory from the 18th century to the late 1890s. When justifying his belief in a lunar atmosphere, Pfaall draws on the observations of Johann Hieronymus Schröter, Johannes Hevelius, and Giovanni Domenico Cassini that suggested its existence. By citing contemporary astronomers and their speculative theories, and thinking about how they would apply to a voyage to the Moon, Poe gave the concept of spaceflight a new basis in science. By citing contemporary astronomers and their speculative theories, and thinking about how they would apply to a voyage to the Moon, Poe gave the concept of spaceflight a new basis in science. In some respects, however, Poe’s insights into the psychological and behavioral characteristics that would lead to spaceflight were even more insightful than his clever applications of contemporary astronomy. Although he is still working within the lone-inventor model employed by Godwin and Tucker, the inventor is no longer an aristocratic adventurer, an extraterrestrial, or a mystic scientist, but rather a simple engineer — Hans Pfaall, an underemployed and debt-ridden Dutch bellows maker in Rotterdam. Even more significantly, this inventor begins to approach the level of single-minded obsession and dedication of effort and resources that would possess many of the early pioneers of spaceflight. Like many of them, Pfaall has an almost epiphanic spaceflight inspiration after reading a book — in this case, Speculative Astronomy by Professor Encke: “There were some particular passages which affected my imagination in an extraordinary manner. The longer I meditated upon these, the more intense grew the interest which had been excited within me. items.title: Field Guide to Predators in Their Natural Habitat
items.summary: The Photographs Never Develop Like You Imagine I’m a photographer , he said, I want you to pose for me . A camera dangled from his neck instead of a whistle— otherwise he was my dad’s stand-in, blue Oxford tucked into khakis. He found me in the concession line, five bucks sweating in my palm. My mother was cheering on my twin brother’s soccer team; my father was the coach, and the August heat played goal against an unstoppable dark. He steered me to the swings, pinching my arm, then to the playground horses, their painted-on eyelashes batting. He posed me how he wanted me seen. From the field I heard my brother starting a fist-fight; when I turned to look, the man shook my chin back into place. Don’t move , his voice like cleats scraping knees. He orbited me, excited electron, saliva foaming at the corners of his mouth as he shot. Good girl . I didn’t correct him, his camera glared a gleam. He fixed me atop the jungle gym; when ordered, I hung inverted, Like a Princess transforming into a bat . His lens stiffened from its cave. Shutterstun of clicks. I struggled to right myself. After, he bought a Kit Kat we shared behind the stand. His thumb slid chocolate across my cheek, my last picture. He walked me into view, finger jabbing my spine forward, to where a referee was handing my offsides brother a red card. My mother jotted our address on a used roster. Before he left, he said, You have such a beautiful daughter . In the van, my mother said, Don’t go missing like that . The next day, she shaved my head. I watched the mailbox but nothing ever came. I never saw the girl he took again. Junior Scientist Summer Camp That June we were scientists, bluing liquids in our beakers, iodinating slides to illuminate the interior lives of basil, gluing bisected stamens into our starter field guides. We wore test-tube toolbelts to collect stream samples; I used mine like a sash since it wouldn’t fit my waist. Misty Mills dubbed me Nerd Rambo, but Andrea Gerber’s nickname stuck: Miss Obesity, 1989. I was fixed in their binocular crosshairs after that. Every day, we returned to Maitland Middle School’s laboratories, composition pages full, feeling older, on the brink of discovery. I rode in the back of the bus, self-exiled, my fat body jostling from the rural roads. Igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic: I memorized the solid world like an alien trying to learn how he fit in the new ecosystem. Then Jeremy Fradin said, Look at his titties bounce! and the boys circled like white coats in a medical theater, eyes wide as magnifying glasses. I was a specimen, my sweating thighs stuck to the leather seat. Damon Bixler cupped my breasts from behind. Mark Collins lifted my shirt. I sent my mind into the passing orange groves in full fruit. I stayed still while anonymous hands took turns to twist. Like radio dials , a voice as far away as Venus said. I heard the girls giggling from farther galaxies. I practiced reciting in my head: krypton, xenon, boron, argon, neon, the gases once called inert and which we now call noble because of their impenetrable electron shells. The post Field Guide to Predators in Their Natural Habitat appeared first on Electric Literature .

items.title: Naturalness: a useful principle, but not an absolute rule
items.summary: There are two classes of problems that physicists often talk about that might leave you thinking, “geez, a physicist can never be satisfied, can they?” The first is called a coincidence problem: where things that have no apparent reason for being close together actually are close together. Examples include: the normal matter and dark matter densities, the cosmic matter density and the dark energy density, the total energy of the Hoyle state of carbon-12 being almost exactly equal to the rest mass energy of three helium-4 nuclei, or Dirac’s large number coincidence , where the strength of gravity is approximately equal to the inverse of the age of the Universe since the Big Bang. The second is the opposite type of problem, known as a hierarchy problem: where it seems like there is a large, unnatural, inexplicable gap between things that — if everything were equal — you might expect to be close together. Examples of that include: the huge differences between the electroweak scale and the Planck scale, the huge difference in the strength between gravity and electromagnetism, the big difference between the mass of most of the massive particles in the Standard Model and the tiny masses of neutrinos, or the cosmological constant problem, arguably the largest-magnitude mismatch of them all. You might think that having both “coincidence” and “hierarchy” problems just means that physicists are always looking for trouble, and can never be satisfied. But both sets of problems are just the extreme poles of fine-tuning, and naturalness is one often (but not always) useful way to approach it. Here’s what the big idea is all about. Explanatory diagram showing how symmetry breaking works. At a high enough energy level, a ball settled in the center (lowest point), and the result has symmetry. At lower energy levels, the center becomes unstable, the ball rolls to a lower point – but in doing so, it settles on an (arbitrary) position and the result is that symmetry is broken – the resulting position is not symmetrical. An outcome that may seem unlikely can be made sense of if the history of the system, and a mechanism that naturally leads to that seemingly unlikely outcome, can be correctly identified. Credit : FT2/Wikimedia Commons The study of the Universe itself — both in terms of the fundamental laws that govern it as well as the ingredients that make it up — is, by definition, the study of nature. Assuming that we, as humans, can intuit what is itself “natural” is kind of a bit of hubris on our part: nature simply is what it is, and we, ourselves a product of nature, can only hope to figure out what it is and how it got to be this way. And yet, it’s been an incredibly successful approach at times. A “natural” idea simply posits the following: When we find two quantities that are close together, but don’t appear to be related, we ask what sort of relationship could exist that would lead to those quantities matching (or nearly matching) one another. And when we find two quantities that we might expect to be close together, but that instead turn out to be very far apart, we ask what sort of mechanism could exist for leading to those quantities having such a severe mismatch in reality. In other words, the idea of naturalness is simply to state that instead of the Universe just being the way it is, full of coincidences, huge disparities, and all sorts of “fine-tunings” that had to occur for it to turn out the way it did, there ought to be mechanisms in place that led to it being the way we observe it to be. Balanced Rock, shown here in photos from before 1975 (black and white) and after 1976 (color), showcases how weathering and erosion can lead to the collapse of structures over time. At right, the structure once known as “Chip off the Old Block” fell during the winter of 1975-1976, and someday, Balanced Rock will fall as well. However, it was created by natural processes, even if it doesn’t appear so; understanding how is the key to solving what appears, on the surface, to be a fine-tuning problem. Credits : National Parks Service/Neal Herbert Throughout the history of theoretical physics, and in particular during the development of the Standard Models of particle physics and cosmology throughout the 20th century, this approach turned out to often be incredibly useful. In the early days of quantum physics, people started asking questions about the electric field that surrounded the electron and how you could reconcile that with a point-like particle, which experiments supported. If you calculated the total electrostatic energy stored in an electric field created by a charged “point,” you’d get a catastrophic answer: an infinite amount of energy. But this isn’t possible; we know that the electron has a finite, observed rest mass, and that therefore the total energy of the electron can be no greater than the value given by E = mc² , where m is the mass of the electron. This puzzle, of the electron’s self-energy , led to the development of a whole new field to get a finite answer rather than the unnatural, infinite one that was classically predicted: quantum field theory . Along with that development came a novel prediction, the existence of an antimatter particle that was oppositely charged to the electron, the positron , and eventually the development of quantum electrodynamics. The so-called ‘Dirac sea’ arose from solving the Dirac equation, based on a complex vector space, which yielded both positive and negative energy solutions. The negative solutions were soon identified with antimatter, and the positron (antielectron) in particular opened up an entire new world for particle physics. Credit : Incnis Mrsi / PUBLIC DOMAIN In nuclear physics, there was a puzzle that arose when it came to the generation of the elements in the Universe: the puzzle of carbon. We were able, even in the 1950s, to easily measure the rest mass energy of the different elements and their isotopes, including: hydrogen (with a single proton as its nucleus), helium (with helium-4, with two protons and two neutrons as its nucleus being the most abundant), and carbon (with carbon-12, with six protons and six neutrons, being the most common version). But if stars were the dominant source of carbon in the Universe, then there was a problem that arose: the mass of carbon-12 was too mismatched, given the properties of the interiors of stars, from the mass of the three helium-4 nuclei, combined, that must go into creating it. So how was carbon made? It was by thinking along this line that Fred Hoyle hypothesized a natural solution to this problem, and a mechanism by which carbon-12 could be created in the necessary abundance: he theorized the existence of a new, excited state for carbon-12 nuclei whose energy was exactly (or almost exactly) equal to the rest mass energy of three helium-4 nuclei combined. This state, the Hoyle state , was later observed by nuclear physicist Willie Fowler, marking a remarkable success for the naturalness approach. If the value of that excited state of carbon-12, which turned out to be a 7.654 MeV resonance, were different in energy by even 5%, our Universe wouldn’t have made the carbon that enabled our existence. The prediction of the Hoyle State, an excited state of a carbon-12 nucleus, and the discovery of the triple-alpha process is perhaps the most stunningly successful use of anthropic reasoning in scientific history. If the mass of the excited state of carbon-12 were even 5% more or less energetic than its value above the ground state, we would make too little carbon to explain the abundance observed in our Universe. items.title: A Novel That Turns the Tables on AI
items.summary: What’s the point of playing? Games don’t provide an organism with food, water, or shelter. They distract from the pursuit of survival and reproduction. And yet play is found across the animal kingdom; the act separates creative, joyful, living creatures from “merely mechanical things,” as the Dutch historian and cultural theorist Johan Huizinga once put it. In his famous 1938 study on games and play, Homo Ludens , Huizinga asserts that the behavior represents something fundamentally absurd: Humans “play and know that we play, so we must be more than merely rational beings, for play is irrational.” Huizinga’s analytical understanding of leisure remains influential in the fields of philosophy and game design. Perhaps this is why the British writer Joanna Kavenna, halfway through her zany, cerebral romp of a novel, Seven , quotes at length from Huizinga. Play is necessary, she quotes him as saying, even if “we live in a demented world.” Humans aren’t robots, Kavenna seems to be reminding us. And her novel, which lands during a moment when the biggest question about robots is whether they’ll kill us all, offers a jaunty insight: When we embrace our irrationality, we deepen our understanding of what separates us from our computers. The plot and thematic structure of Seven are guided by an invented board game, Seven, which resembles chess and involves a spiral-shaped board known as the “box.” The game involves seven movable pieces and two six-sided dice, and its rules are flexible; the novel itself is punctuated by four separate sets of instructions. (This slipperiness will become important later on.) In the same way that chess has been used by writers and artists as a metaphor for war or existential struggle, Seven becomes a symbol for how humans attempt to make sense of their world’s incoherence. Kavenna’s characters are deadly serious about their game, but the author is willing to poke fun at them. The action begins in a university philosophy department in Oslo, where the nameless, genderless narrator works as a research assistant to an Icelandic philosopher named Alda Jónsdóttir. The professor’s area of study is called “box philosophy,” and it focuses on the problem of “Thinking Outside the Box About Thinking Outside the Box.” What does the assistant’s job look like in practice? They spend time getting too drunk at faculty dinner parties, doing menial work for Jónsdóttir, and “asking questions,” but their first matter of serious business is “working on none of the above.” They try to clarify: “I don’t mean that I didn’t work on anything I’ve just mentioned, but that I worked on the category of None of the Above .” This deadpan joke serves a narrative function, priming the assistant—and the reader—to start thinking beyond the rules, and to enter a more expansive realm. [ Read: Open AI just carpet-bombed mathematics ] Jónsdóttir sends the narrator away on, essentially, a wild-goose chase to Greece; their mission is to hunt down a man named Theódoros Apostolakis—a poet, dentist, and Seven enthusiast who is “big in boxes.” This journey across Europe includes several professional Seven competitions, during which the rules keep changing. Everything the assistant learned in Norway seems useless except the central lesson—to think outside the box. These games abroad lead the narrator to start contemplating the role of recreation, the limits of human ingenuity, and the meaning of consciousness. Soon this will bring them face-to-face with the novel’s ultimate threat, an artificial-intelligence program that undermines everything that Jónsdóttir and the Seven players care about: creativity, curiosity, play. “How do you play a game without rules?” Kavenna writes. “Do you just make stuff up and hope for the best?” These thoughts coalesce in the second half of the novel, when an AI bot named the Quail is introduced. Invented by a Seven player named Indrek Laar, who, Kavenna pointedly notes, believes that “AI was very clever and therefore had experiences,” the Quail is named for qualia , a term borrowed from philosophy. (It’s meant to capture a quality of consciousness, though the narrator dismisses it as “a baroque way of saying ‘experience.’”) The bot is “designed to play Seven” and nothing else, Kavenna writes. “It couldn’t give you relationship advice or sympathise when you were feeling sad, or translate the Iliad or write your homework. It just played Seven.” And it does its job well. The Quail manages to beat the world’s reigning Seven champion, Ashok Deo, in a humiliating match that the narrator calls both the “greatest Seven game of the millennium” and “the worst game ever”—technically impressive, but absolutely demoralizing. “No one had enjoyed it,” Kavenna writes, “because the Quail couldn’t experience enjoyment and the Quail’s proxy—Indrek Laar—was horrified.” Ashok’s loss echoes real-life incidents in which computers have won games against humans, such as the 1997 victory of IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer over the chess grandmaster Garry Kasparov and the repeated defeats of the Go champion Lee Sedol by Google’s program AlphaGo in 2016. Culturally, these results represented a significant shift in how we understand the relationship between humans and computers. The Kasparov match “had the impact of a Greek tragedy ,” one audience member told The New York Times . But its reception wasn’t all bad: Another champion commented, “Nice style!” while watching Deep Blue take another round. The machine, she admitted to the Times , “made many moves that were based on understanding chess, on feeling the position. We all thought computers couldn’t do that.” Deep Blue, and AlphaGo after it, seemed to do more than just win by brute force: They encroached on the human flair for creativity. [ Read: Yet another literary prizewinner seems to be AI ] Those machines—and the fears they inspired—can look quaint when compared with today’s technology. Some AI-safety researchers see it as an existential threat to humankind. Earlier this year, an OpenAI model not meant to have open access to the internet managed to break out of its “sandbox” and hack the databases of another tech company, Hugging Face . Cyberattacks are becoming more sophisticated and more prevalent . AI-company employees are publicly quitting , raising alarms about the safety culture inside major firms. Popular conversations are inundated by pessimism—and at the same time, companies are advertising their services by urging onlookers to “stop hiring humans,” as in one controversial San Francisco– and New York–based billboard campaign . The stakes of the conflict between human and computer capabilities can feel bleak and funereal. Kavenna’s portrayal of the battle of man versus machine is leavened, however, by her sense of humor. Machines may be able to beat us, but has a computer ever written an effective joke? Beyond being funny, the novel also defies machines by eschewing binaries (“I was neither one thing nor another,” the genderless, nameless, race-less narrator observes of their mental state. “I was mostly in a state of / .”) But Kavenna’s pitch for human superiority really comes together in the novel’s denouement. Eventually, the narrator meets a Seven champion named Eleni Hikaru Jones. She’ll point out that when Deep Blue beat Kasparov, the latter “carried on playing the game. He accepted that Deep Blue was better than him, but he was still the best human player.” This idea inspires the characters to one-up machine intelligence by changing the rules of the game—or, in Kavenna’s framing, thinking outside the box. While Ashok plays the Quail, Indrek, the bot’s inventor, recognizes the turmoil he’s unleashed. Human loneliness, not malice, was his motive: “He made the Quail so he would always have someone to play with.” Knowing this, Eleni persuades Indrek to join forces with her. items.title: Why your cat is the best philosopher
items.summary: A young girl looks out of the classroom window. It’s the end of the day, and she’s bored. She spots a goldfinch land on the ground outside. It hops about and twitches for whatever reasons goldfinches do that, and then takes off. It swoops and dives around the playground, as if doing it all for the girl. Oh, how she would like to fly. Humans have long looked to the animal kingdom for inspiration. We envy their skills and talents: flight, speed, strength, sociability, and so on. Religions almost always feature animal imagery, and flags will often blazon a lion, an eagle, a wolf — something bold or heroic. And philosophers are in on the game as well. Even in the earliest historical records, people were exploring the philosophical side of animals. What can this animal teach me? What virtues does it embody? What can I learn about myself by studying this creature? Joining in an ancient line is John Gray’s book Feline Philosophy . In the book, Gray examines what we can all learn about life from spending more time around cats. His conclusion: We should all be a bit more feline. Mo the Philosophical Cat A cat does not do philosophy, and that makes it a better philosopher than anyone else. Gray argues that for humans, philosophy acts as a kind of medicine. We are full of doubt and anxiety about how to live, yes, but most of all we are filled with the existential dread that comes from knowing that we will die. To combat this, we create systems like religions and ideologies. We try to soothe our death-terror with stories. We become obsessed with “the good life,” “the examined life,” and “time well spent.” We have turned the word “happiness” into a multi-billion-dollar industry, but as a species we are no happier than we ever were. We are sick, craving a cure, but the medicine we have isn’t working. Cats, though, have no such sickness. Imagine a cat called Mo. Mo does not search for meaning in her life, and she is not trying to become a better cat. She does not experience her life as a project that could fail, and she doesn’t wake up with the imagined burden of a thousand cats’ expectations. Mo hunts, she sleeps, and she sits in the sunlight. When she suffers, she does not add to her suffering by asking why. She does not need to invent systems or stories because the world is as the world is. Gray’s point is not that Mo is wise; Mo wouldn’t write books even if she could. The point is that Mo is not sick. Humans are. Be more cat Gray starts his book by saying that we cannot become a cat. We can try to transfigure if we want, but you’re mostly running up against the immovable wall of cellular biology. Still, we can mimic a cat. We can do more cat things and try to see things like a cat. Gray leans on a point that Blaise Pascal makes about ritual and religion: If you do something enough, it changes you. If you force your mind a certain way, it stays like that. As the philosopher Mark Vorobej pointed out, it’s not entirely clear why Gray has singled out cats. What’s true here of cats is true of dogs, birds, rats, squirrels, moles, badgers, or mongooses. Should we be more mongoose? It’s a fair critique, but it is somewhat pedantic. I’m sure Gray is not some feline exceptionalist. I take his book to be a lesson in intentionality. We can try to become more like a cat, rat, or badger, and I think he chose cats because they’re both cute and far more present in our lives. We see cats at home or on social media. All over social media. It’s just much easier to talk about something so available. Yes, he could have chosen dogs, but hey — take your pick. So, how can we be more cat? Well, we need to distance ourselves from this sick and broken human way of seeing things. Stop seeing your lives in terms of some huge, overarching metanarrative. Don’t try to find meaning in your suffering. Stop seeing the world in terms of puzzles to solve. Don’t try to persuade other people to be more reasonable. Recognize that you are who you are, and it is what it is. Sometimes life just happens. So climb trees, play with a ball, sleep a lot more, and lie by the fire when things get cold and dark. Cherish life and think only as much as you want. This article Why your cat is the best philosopher is featured on Big Think .
